title: Getting around the city: seven short texts
texts: Anyone who has ever searched for coins at a ticket machine will appreciate the modern travel pass. One plastic card, topped up online, is accepted on trams, buses and the underground alike, and the system calculates the cheapest fare automatically at the end of the day. Regular passengers say they no longer think about the cost of each ride, only about where they want to go.

The newest buses in several cities run on batteries instead of diesel. They are nearly silent, and nothing comes out of the exhaust pipe, so the smell that used to hang around bus stops has disappeared. Local officials hope that ordinary cars will follow the example in the future, although the high price of the vehicles means that renewal will take many years.

In a city where traffic often crawls, many commuters have discovered that the quickest way to the office is also the cheapest one. Hire bikes are waiting in racks on almost every corner, and a short journey of three or four kilometres takes less time than a bus. Cyclists glide past rows of stationary cars, arrive without a parking problem and, as a bonus, get some exercise on the way.

In the old centre, traffic is banned from nine in the morning until late evening. Where lorries and cars used to fight for space, there are now benches, flower beds and the tables of small cafés. Shop owners feared they would lose customers, but turnover has actually grown, because people who walk slowly look at windows and stop for a coffee. The air in these narrow streets is cleaner, too.

Between eight and nine in the morning, the picture on many platforms is the same: people stand shoulder to shoulder, and the first carriage that arrives is already too full to board. Passengers let one train pass, then another, form a long queue at the stairs and finally push their way in, holding their bags above their heads. Some companies now let staff start later, which spreads the load across the morning.

For a passenger in a wheelchair or with a pushchair, a staircase can be a wall. That is why newer stations are fitted with lifts, buses have low floors with ramps, and announcements are made aloud as well as shown on screens, which helps people with poor sight. Engineers add that these changes benefit everybody, from parents with luggage to tourists who simply cannot read the signs.

A decade ago you had to phone a dispatcher and hope for the best. Now a few taps on a smartphone summon a driver who is already nearby, and the screen shows both the car and the price. The fare rises when many people want to go home at once, and some passengers resent it, but few would go back to waiting at the roadside.
discuss: How do you usually get around your city or town? What would you improve?
Would you like trams or bike-sharing in your town? Why or why not?
Should cities ban cars from the centre? Give arguments for and against.
